concept.name: Decentralized exchange
concept.definition: A decentralized exchange (DEX) is a trading venue implemented as smart contracts — usually an automated market maker — that lets users swap tokens directly from their own wallets without depositing funds with an intermediary.
concept.intuition: A DEX is a currency-exchange kiosk run by code: open 24/7 to anyone, and your money never leaves your pocket until the exact moment of the swap.
concept.mechanics: Traders interact directly with on-chain liquidity pools (e.g. Uniswap) whose smart contracts price and settle swaps atomically in a single transaction; liquidity is supplied by other users earning fees. DEXs are permissionless — anyone can trade, provide liquidity, or list a market — and non-custodial, unlike order-book venues that hold user deposits.
concept.failure_modes: Public mempool exposure invites sandwich attacks and worse execution than quoted; shallow pools give huge price impact; unaudited or malicious token contracts and rug-pull pools are common because listing is permissionless.
concept.misconceptions: DEX prices are not set by an order book of other people's bids/asks (in AMM designs) but by pool ratios, and they track external markets only through arbitrageurs. 'Decentralized' does not mean risk-free — smart contract exploits and MEV are native hazards.
concept.example: Swapping 1 ETH for USDC on Uniswap executes entirely within one Ethereum transaction against the ETH/USDC pool: you sign the swap, the pool contract computes the output via x·y=k, and the USDC lands directly in your wallet.
